about: A large aromatic shrub or small tree widely found across South and Southeast Asia. It has woody, branched stems with greyish-brown bark. The leaves are opposite and compound, typically with five lance-shaped leaflets — green above and greyish beneath from fine hairs. Small bluish-purple flowers appear in terminal panicles, followed by small round blackish drupes. Every part of the plant carries a distinctive herbal fragrance from its essential oils.

uses.label: Anti-inflammatory
uses.description: Leaves and bark are used in traditional remedies to reduce joint pain, arthritis, and swelling.

uses.label: Insect repellent
uses.description: Dried leaves are placed in stored grain and cupboards to keep insects away.

uses.label: Wound healing
uses.description: Leaf paste is applied externally on wounds, boils, and skin disorders.

uses.label: Respiratory support
uses.description: Used in Ayurvedic medicine for coughs, colds, and respiratory congestion.

uses.label: Fever management
uses.description: Decoctions of the leaves are traditionally employed as an antipyretic.

funFacts.question: Why is it called five-leaved?
funFacts.answer: The species name 'negundo' refers to its typically five-foliolate leaf arrangement, though some varieties may have three leaflets.

funFacts.question: A natural pharmacy
funFacts.answer: Nirgundi is one of the most versatile plants in Ayurveda — it appears in formulations for over 50 different conditions.

funFacts.question: Leaves that smell
funFacts.answer: The strong aromatic smell of crushed leaves comes from volatile essential oils rich in terpenoids, which also give it insect-repelling properties.

warnings.headline: Generally safe when used as directed

about: A small aromatic evergreen tree native to the Indian subcontinent, the curry tree is best known for its highly fragrant pinnate leaves, each bearing 11 to 21 pairs of ovate-lanceolate leaflets. The bark is greyish-brown and rough. Small, white, fragrant flowers appear in clusters, maturing into shiny black berries. The leaves release their characteristic curry aroma when crushed, making them one of the most beloved culinary herbs in South Asian cooking.

uses.label: Culinary spice
uses.description: Fresh or dried leaves are tempered in hot oil to release flavour — a cornerstone of South Indian, Sri Lankan, and Southeast Asian cuisines.

uses.label: Digestive health
uses.description: Traditionally chewed raw or brewed as tea to improve digestion and relieve stomach disorders.

uses.label: Diabetes management
uses.description: Used in traditional herbal preparations to help regulate blood sugar levels.

uses.label: Hair care
uses.description: Leaf extracts are a popular ingredient in hair oils and tonics to support healthy hair growth.

uses.label: Antimicrobial
uses.description: The carbazole alkaloids in the leaves show strong antimicrobial activity in laboratory studies.

funFacts.question: Not the same as curry powder
funFacts.answer: Despite the name, curry leaves are not an ingredient in curry powder — that spice blend is a British invention. Fresh curry leaves are used for tempering, a completely different technique.

funFacts.question: A nutritional powerhouse
funFacts.answer: Curry leaves are rich in vitamin A, vitamin C, calcium, iron, and phosphorus — far more than most culinary herbs.

funFacts.question: Named after a botanist
funFacts.answer: The genus Murraya honours Johan Andreas Murray, an 18th-century Swedish botanist and student of Linnaeus.

warnings.headline: Extremely bitter — not for casual use

about: An annual herb with erect, branched, quadrangular stems reaching up to 90 cm. Its simple, opposite, lanceolate leaves are intensely bitter — hence the name King of Bitters. Small white flowers with purple markings bloom in axillary and terminal clusters, producing narrow elongated capsules filled with numerous tiny seeds. Kalmegh is one of the most important medicinal plants in Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine, valued primarily for its hepatoprotective and immunomodulatory properties.

uses.label: Liver protection
uses.description: The primary Ayurvedic use — andrographolide has well-documented hepatoprotective effects and is a key ingredient in liver tonics.

uses.label: Fever & infections
uses.description: Traditionally used for viral and bacterial infections, colds, coughs, and respiratory tract disorders.

uses.label: Immunity booster
uses.description: Its immunomodulatory properties make it a popular remedy during seasonal illness.

uses.label: Digestive aid
uses.description: Stimulates appetite and improves digestion despite (or because of) its intense bitterness.

funFacts.question: How bitter is it really?
funFacts.answer: It's called the King of Bitters for good reason — andrographolide is one of the most bitter naturally occurring compounds known, and the whole plant tastes extraordinarily sharp.

funFacts.question: A pandemic-era star
funFacts.answer: Kalmegh saw a huge surge in global interest during the COVID-19 pandemic as researchers investigated its antiviral and immunomodulatory properties.

funFacts.question: Used in two great traditions
funFacts.answer: It's one of the few plants extensively used in both Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine, known as Chuan Xin Lian in TCM.

warnings.headline: Generally safe externally; internal use requires caution

sunlight.label: Sunlight
sunlight.value: Bright indirect light to partial sun

water.label: Water
water.value: Low — let soil dry between watering

about: A perennial succulent herb known for its extraordinary ability to propagate vegetatively — tiny plantlets grow along the scalloped leaf margins, drop off, and root wherever they land, earning it the name Life Plant or Miracle Leaf. Its thick, fleshy leaves are ovate and opposite. Pendulous, tubular reddish-purple flowers hang in terminal clusters like cathedral bells. Native to Madagascar, it has naturalised throughout the tropics and is widely used in folk medicine, particularly for kidney stones and wound healing.

uses.label: Kidney stone support
uses.description: Leaf juice is a well-known folk remedy for kidney stones — the name Patharchatta literally means 'stone-breaker' in Hindi.

uses.label: Wound healing
uses.description: Crushed leaves are applied topically on wounds, burns, cuts, and insect bites to speed healing.

uses.label: Anti-inflammatory
uses.description: Used externally and internally in traditional medicine to reduce swelling and inflammation.

uses.label: Cough & fever
uses.description: Leaf extracts are used in folk preparations for respiratory ailments and fever reduction.

funFacts.question: How does it make babies on its leaves?
funFacts.answer: This phenomenon is called vegetative vivipary — meristematic tissue along the leaf margin develops into complete miniature plantlets complete with roots, which detach and grow independently.

funFacts.question: A survivor's strategy
funFacts.answer: Its succulent leaves store water, allowing it to survive long dry spells — and the plantlets ensure it colonises new ground without needing seeds.

funFacts.question: Also called Goethe Plant
funFacts.answer: The German poet Goethe was fascinated by this plant's reproductive strategy and wrote about it in his scientific essays.

warnings.headline: Generally safe when used as directed

water.label: Water
water.value: High — thrives in wet / boggy soil

about: A small creeping perennial herb with soft, branched, prostrate stems that root at the nodes. Its opposite leaves are simple, fleshy, oval-shaped, and sessile. Small white to pale-blue flowers with purple veins appear solitarily, maturing into tiny capsules. Brahmi thrives in wet, marshy habitats across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Revered in Ayurveda for over 3,000 years, it is the premier intellect-enhancing herb, named after Lord Brahma, the creator in Hindu mythology, symbolising its power to enhance consciousness.

uses.label: Memory & cognition
uses.description: The best-known Ayurvedic nootropic — used to enhance memory, learning, concentration, and mental clarity.

uses.label: Stress & anxiety
uses.description: Its adaptogenic and anxiolytic properties make it a cornerstone of stress-management herbal formulations.

uses.label: Nervous system support
uses.description: Used for neurological conditions including epilepsy support, with bacosides showing neuroprotective effects in studies.

uses.label: Skin disorders
uses.description: Paste of the fresh plant is applied to inflammatory skin conditions and wounds.

funFacts.question: Named after a god
funFacts.answer: The name Brahmi comes from Brahma, the Hindu god of creation — the plant is believed to enhance sattvic (pure, creative) qualities of the mind.

funFacts.question: Fish love it too
funFacts.answer: Brahmi is a popular aquarium and pond plant — it oxygenates water and provides shelter for small fish and amphibians.

funFacts.question: 3,000 years of use
funFacts.answer: References to Brahmi appear in the Charaka Samhita, one of the foundational texts of Ayurveda written around 1000 BCE.

warnings.headline: Generally safe when used as directed

about: A small creeping perennial herb with slender green stems that root at the nodes, forming dense mats in moist habitats. Its distinctive round to kidney-shaped peltate leaves on long petioles channel rainwater to the roots — a clever adaptation. Small pinkish-white flowers cluster in umbels, producing flattened schizocarpic fruits. Found across tropical Asia, Africa, and Australia, Gotu Kola has been a cornerstone of Ayurvedic, Traditional Chinese, and Southeast Asian medicine for centuries, prized as a brain tonic and wound healer.

uses.label: Brain tonic
uses.description: Used in Ayurveda and TCM to enhance memory, concentration, and cognitive function — often paired with Brahmi.

uses.label: Wound healing
uses.description: Asiaticoside and madecassoside promote collagen synthesis, making Gotu Kola extracts popular in wound-healing creams and scar treatments.

uses.label: Skin health
uses.description: Widely used in cosmetic products for its skin-protective, soothing, and anti-ageing properties.

uses.label: Stress & anxiety
uses.description: Traditional herbal preparations use it to calm the mind and reduce mental fatigue.

funFacts.question: Elephant wisdom
funFacts.answer: Gotu Kola is popularly associated with elephants in folklore — the belief is that elephants, known for their long memory, eat it to stay sharp. There's even a saying: 'A leaf a day keeps old age away.'

funFacts.question: Nature's umbrella
funFacts.answer: The round peltate leaves are shaped like tiny umbrellas — the long petiole attaches at the centre of the leaf blade, channelling rainwater directly to the roots.

funFacts.question: A tale of two tonics
funFacts.answer: Gotu Kola (Centella asiatica) and Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri) are often confused — both are called brain tonics, but they're completely different plants from different families.

warnings.headline: Generally safe when used as directed

about: A perennial herb prized for its fleshy, spindle-shaped, white tuberous roots — the most valuable part of the plant. Its narrow, lanceolate leaves form a basal rosette, while small white star-shaped flowers bloom on slender stalks. The roots are rich in saponins (up to 14%), among the highest of any Indian medicinal plant. Native to central and western India, Safed Musli is one of the most commercially important medicinal plants in Ayurveda, valued primarily as a rejuvenating tonic and adaptogen. Due to high demand, it is classified as Near Threatened.

uses.label: Rejuvenating tonic
uses.description: Used as a general health tonic and rasayana in Ayurveda to build strength, stamina, and vitality.

uses.label: Adaptogen
uses.description: Helps the body cope with physical and mental stress — widely used in herbal formulations for fatigue and weakness.

uses.label: Immune support
uses.description: The saponins and polysaccharides in the roots have immunomodulatory properties.

uses.label: Muscle strength
uses.description: Traditionally used by athletes and bodybuilders in herbal preparations to support muscle development and recovery.

funFacts.question: Why is it called white musli?
funFacts.answer: The harvested roots are peeled to reveal a pure white interior — 'safed' means white in Hindi, and the roots resemble the colour of bleached muslin cloth.

funFacts.question: A saponin champion
funFacts.answer: The roots contain up to 14% saponins by dry weight — one of the highest concentrations found in any medicinal plant, which explains its potent bioactivity.

funFacts.question: Cultivation is critical
funFacts.answer: Wild populations have declined sharply due to overharvesting. Today, most commercial Safed Musli comes from organised cultivation to protect wild stocks.

warnings.headline: Generally safe when used as directed

about: A medium-sized deciduous tree with light grey to brown exfoliating bark. Its small, light-green leaves are closely arranged along branchlets, giving the foliage a feathery appearance. Small greenish-yellow flowers appear in clusters, maturing into smooth, round, pale greenish-yellow fruits with six distinct lobes. Amla is one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C — with 20 to 30 times more than oranges — and its vitamin C is stabilised by tannins so it survives drying and cooking. Revered in Ayurveda as a premier rasayana (rejuvenating tonic), it is among the most important medicinal plants in the Indian subcontinent.

uses.label: Immunity booster
uses.description: The exceptionally high vitamin C content makes Amla a cornerstone of immune-support herbal formulations like Chyawanprash.

uses.label: Digestive health
uses.description: Fresh fruit, dried powder, or juice is used to improve digestion, relieve acidity, and support liver function.

uses.label: Hair & skin care
uses.description: Amla oil and powder are widely used in hair oils, shampoos, and face packs for their nourishing and antioxidant properties.

uses.label: Cardiometabolic support
uses.description: Studies suggest Amla helps regulate blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure — supporting heart and metabolic health.

funFacts.question: Vitamin C that doesn't fade
funFacts.answer: Unlike most fruits, Amla's vitamin C is remarkably stable — the high tannin content protects it from oxidation, so even dried and powdered Amla retains its potency.

funFacts.question: The sacred tree
funFacts.answer: In Hindu tradition, the Amla tree is considered sacred — it's believed that Lord Vishnu resides in it, and worshipping the tree on Amla Navami brings prosperity.

funFacts.question: Chyawanprash's star ingredient
funFacts.answer: Amla is the primary ingredient in Chyawanprash, one of the oldest and most famous Ayurvedic formulations, traditionally made from over 40 herbs.

warnings.headline: Generally safe when used as directed

about: A large evergreen tree with rough, flaky grey to dark-brown bark. Its opposite leaves are leathery, glossy, and oval to lance-shaped, dotted with aromatic oil glands. Small, fragrant greenish-white flowers bloom in clusters, giving way to oval fleshy berries that ripen from green to deep purple-black. The fruit's deep-purple juice is rich in anthocyanins and stains the tongue for hours — a childhood memory for millions across South Asia. Jamun has been used for centuries in Ayurveda, particularly the seeds, which are valued for their antidiabetic properties.

uses.label: Diabetes management
uses.description: Jamun seed powder is one of the most well-known Ayurvedic remedies for managing blood sugar — the compound jamboline is believed to slow starch-to-sugar conversion.

uses.label: Digestive health
uses.description: The fruit, bark, and seeds are used in traditional remedies for diarrhoea, dysentery, and other digestive complaints.

uses.label: Antioxidant
uses.description: The deep-purple anthocyanins in the fruit are potent antioxidants that help combat oxidative stress.

uses.label: Oral health
uses.description: Bark decoctions are traditionally used as a mouthwash for gum health and oral ulcers.

funFacts.question: The tongue-staining fruit
funFacts.answer: The deep-purple juice stains the tongue for hours after eating — a familiar childhood experience for millions across the Indian subcontinent. Those same anthocyanins are powerful antioxidants.

funFacts.question: A tree that lives a century
funFacts.answer: Jamun trees can live over 100 years, and some specimens in India are estimated to be several centuries old, still producing fruit.

funFacts.question: The seed is the medicine
funFacts.answer: While the fruit is eaten fresh, it's the seed that holds the real medicinal value — dried and powdered Jamun seeds are a mainstay of Ayurvedic diabetes management.

warnings.headline: Two medicines in one leaf — use carefully

about: A perennial succulent herb with thick, fleshy, green, lance-shaped leaves arranged in a rosette, their serrated margins tapering to sharp points. Yellow tubular flowers rise on long spikes. The leaf contains two distinct medicinal products: the clear inner gel (rich in polysaccharides like acemannan, used for wound healing and skin care) and the yellow latex from the rind (containing anthraquinones like aloin, a potent natural laxative). One of the oldest documented medicinal plants, Aloe vera appears in Sumerian clay tablets from 2200 BCE and has been cultivated across warm regions worldwide for millennia.

uses.label: Skin care & burns
uses.description: The clear gel is applied directly to minor burns, cuts, sunburn, and skin irritations — its cooling, moisturising, and wound-healing properties are well-documented.

uses.label: Cosmetics
uses.description: Aloe gel is a ubiquitous ingredient in moisturisers, shampoos, lotions, and sunscreens for its hydrating and soothing effects.

uses.label: Digestive health
uses.description: The yellow latex (aloin) is a powerful natural laxative — but must be used cautiously due to its potency.

uses.label: Oral health
uses.description: Aloe vera gel is used in some natural toothpastes and mouthwashes for its antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects on gums.

funFacts.question: One leaf, two medicines
funFacts.answer: The same leaf contains two completely different products: the soothing clear inner gel for burns and skin, and the potent yellow latex from the rind — a powerful laxative known since ancient times.

funFacts.question: Used by Cleopatra
funFacts.answer: Legend holds that Cleopatra used Aloe vera as part of her daily beauty regimen — and historical records confirm its use in ancient Egyptian cosmetics and embalming.

funFacts.question: A Sumerian prescription
funFacts.answer: Aloe vera is mentioned on Sumerian clay tablets dating back to 2200 BCE, making it one of the oldest documented medicinal plants in human history.

warnings.headline: Generally safe externally; avoid eye contact

about: A medium to large deciduous tree with rough, grey to dark-brown vertically fissured bark. Its alternate pinnate leaves bear 5 to 10 pairs of lance-shaped leaflets. Small greenish-white flowers form terminal panicles, maturing into round yellowish-brown fleshy drupes — the famous soapnuts. The fruit pericarp is sticky and rich in triterpenoid saponins that produce a natural soap-like lather when mixed with water. Native to the Himalayan foothills and East Asia, Reetha has been used for centuries as a natural cleanser for hair, skin, and delicate fabrics — a zero-waste, biodegradable detergent long before sustainability became mainstream.

uses.label: Natural shampoo
uses.description: The most traditional use — soaked or boiled soapnuts produce a gentle, natural lather that cleanses hair without stripping natural oils.

uses.label: Skin cleanser
uses.description: Used in traditional skincare preparations for eczema, psoriasis, and general cleansing — its antimicrobial properties help with acne and dandruff.

uses.label: Eco-friendly detergent
uses.description: An increasingly popular zero-waste laundry and household cleaner — the saponins are fully biodegradable.

uses.label: Jewellery cleaner
uses.description: Traditionally used to clean delicate gold and silver jewellery without scratching.

funFacts.question: How does a fruit become soap?
funFacts.answer: The fruit pericarp contains triterpenoid saponins — natural surfactants that lower water surface tension and create a lather when agitated. No chemical processing needed.

funFacts.question: Zero-waste before it was a movement
funFacts.answer: Long before sustainability became a buzzword, Indian households used Reetha as a completely biodegradable shampoo, detergent, and cleaner — and the spent shells go right into compost.

funFacts.question: The name says it all
funFacts.answer: The genus name Sapindus comes from Latin 'sapo' (soap) and 'indicus' (Indian) — literally 'soap of India.'

warnings.headline: Generally safe externally; internal use requires caution

about: A large evergreen tree with rough, fissured grey to dark-brown bark that tastes distinctly bitter. Its leaves are alternate and imparipinnate, with 8 to 19 serrated leaflets. Small, white, fragrant flowers bloom in axillary panicles, giving way to smooth oval drupes that ripen from green to yellow — each containing a single seed rich in neem oil. Called the 'Village Pharmacy,' Neem has been a cornerstone of Ayurveda for over 4,000 years. Every part of the tree — leaves, bark, seeds, oil, and even twigs — has medicinal or practical use. The limonoid azadirachtin, unique to Neem, makes it one of the most potent natural insecticides known.

uses.label: Skin care
uses.description: Neem leaf paste and oil are used for acne, eczema, psoriasis, and fungal infections — its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties are among the strongest in the plant kingdom.

uses.label: Dental hygiene
uses.description: Neem twigs have been used as natural toothbrushes (datun) for millennia — neem extracts are now common in herbal toothpaste.

uses.label: Natural pesticide
uses.description: Azadirachtin, unique to Neem, disrupts insect feeding and reproduction — Neem-based biopesticides are used worldwide in organic farming.

uses.label: Hair care
uses.description: Neem oil and leaf extracts are used in hair oils and shampoos to combat dandruff and scalp infections.

funFacts.question: A pharmacy in every village
funFacts.answer: Neem is called the Village Pharmacy because every part of the tree — leaves, bark, seeds, oil, flowers, and twigs — has medicinal value, and a single tree can serve an entire community.

funFacts.question: 4,000 years of documented use
funFacts.answer: Neem appears in the earliest Ayurvedic texts and has been continuously used for over four millennia — few plants can claim such a long and well-documented medicinal history.

funFacts.question: Nature's own insecticide
funFacts.answer: Azadirachtin, the key limonoid in Neem, doesn't kill insects outright — it disrupts their hormonal systems so they stop feeding and can't reproduce, making it remarkably selective and biodegradable.

about: A medium-sized deciduous to semi-evergreen tree renowned for its spectacular display of violet-blue flowers. Its thin, grey to grey-brown bark is rough and slightly fissured. The leaves are opposite and bipinnate — delicate, fern-like, and composed of numerous tiny leaflets that give the canopy a soft, airy texture. Large, fragrant trumpet-shaped flowers in vivid violet-blue to lavender appear in terminal panicles, often blanketing the entire crown before new leaves emerge. Flat, woody, dark-brown capsules follow, releasing thin, winged seeds that scatter on the wind. Native to Argentina and Bolivia, Jacaranda has been planted as an ornamental tree across warm regions worldwide — its breathtaking spring bloom transforms entire streets into tunnels of purple.

uses.label: Ornamental
uses.description: One of the world's most beloved flowering trees — widely planted along streets, in parks, and in gardens for its spectacular seasonal purple display.

uses.label: Folk medicine
uses.description: Leaves and bark are used in traditional medicine in its native range for treating wounds, skin infections, and reducing fever.

uses.label: Shade tree
uses.description: Its broad, airy canopy provides dappled shade, making it a popular choice for avenues and public spaces in warm climates.

uses.label: Woodworking
uses.description: The timber, though not a primary use, is occasionally used for small carpentry and turned items.

funFacts.question: A purple phenomenon
funFacts.answer: When Jacarandas bloom, the entire crown turns violet-blue before new leaves appear — the flowers fall to create a stunning purple carpet beneath the tree, a celebrated event in cities like Pretoria and Sydney.

funFacts.question: Pretoria's purple blanket
funFacts.answer: Pretoria, South Africa, is known as the Jacaranda City — over 70,000 trees line its streets, and each October the city transforms under a spectacular purple canopy.

funFacts.question: A student's superstition
funFacts.answer: At the University of Queensland, students say that if a Jacaranda blossom falls on you during exam season, you'll pass your exams — but if you haven't started studying by the time they bloom, it might already be too late.
